questions.q: How does gradient boosting fundamentally differ from a random forest?
options: Boosting trains trees independently and averages them, just like a random forest
Boosting trains trees sequentially, with each new tree correcting the errors of the ensemble built so far
Boosting can only use linear models, not trees
There is no meaningful difference between the two
questions.explain: Random forests average independently trained trees; gradient boosting builds trees one at a time, each targeting the residual errors left by the previous ones.

questions.q: Why is gradient boosting more prone to overfitting on financial data than a well-tuned random forest?
options: It cannot use regularization at all
Its sequential error-correction keeps chasing whatever pattern remains, including noise, if not carefully controlled
It always uses more features than a random forest
It requires unscaled data
questions.explain: Because each round targets remaining error, an under-regularized boosted model will keep fitting noise round after round, especially when real signal is a tiny fraction of total variance.

questions.q: What does `early_stopping_rounds` do when training an XGBoost or LightGBM model?
options: It randomly removes features during training
It halts training once validation error stops improving for a set number of rounds, rather than relying on a fixed, hand-picked n_estimators
It increases the learning rate automatically
It converts the model to a classifier
questions.explain: Early stopping lets validation performance determine how many boosting rounds are actually useful, instead of guessing a fixed number of estimators.

questions.q: Which combination of settings is generally recommended for boosting on noisy, low-signal financial features?
options: A large learning_rate and very deep trees with no subsampling
A small learning_rate, shallow max_depth, and meaningful subsample/colsample_bytree values
Zero regularization and unlimited n_estimators
Only categorical features with no numeric features
questions.explain: Small learning rates (needing many rounds to overfit), shallow trees, and row/feature subsampling are the primary defenses against overfitting noisy financial data.

questions.q: What do `reg_alpha` and `reg_lambda` control in XGBoost/LightGBM?
options: The number of trees in the ensemble
L1 and L2 regularization penalties applied to the model's leaf weights
The train/test split ratio
The random seed used for bootstrapping
questions.explain: reg_alpha applies an L1 penalty and reg_lambda an L2 penalty on leaf weights, serving a similar regularizing role to the penalties in Ridge/Lasso regression.
